original_question: Is there a finitely presented, or even type F∞ , boundedly acyclic simple orderable group?
target_in_paper: Section 3.3 (“Simple orderable groups”), Question 3.5: “Is there a finitely presented, or even type F∞, boundedly acyclic simple orderable group?”
correct_elements: Your draft is already essentially verbatim to the paper’s official formulation. It correctly captures all four intended features simultaneously: simplicity, orderability, bounded acyclicity, and the two finiteness thresholds singled out in the paper (“finitely presented” and, more strongly, “type F∞”).
missing_details: Use the paper’s exact notation F∞.
Make the existential quantifier explicit: the question is asking whether there exists a group G with all of the listed properties at once.

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, unpack the finiteness notation used immediately above Question 3.5: a group is of type Fn if it admits a K(G,1) with finite n-skeleton, and it is of type F∞ if it is of type Fn for every n.

The paper does not re-define “orderable” inside Section 3.3; a stand-alone version should either keep that term unchanged or specify the intended notion. Nearby Section 6.2 discusses “(left-)orderable” groups and left-orders.
If “boundedly acyclic” is expanded for completeness, one should state the coefficient convention; the nearby bounded-cohomology discussion on the same page uses real coefficients H_b^2(G, R).
refined_question: Does there exist a simple orderable group G that is boundedly acyclic, in the standard sense that H_b^n(G; R) = 0 for all n ≥ 1, and that is either finitely presented or, even more strongly, of type F∞ (equivalently, of type Fn for every n, or admits a K(G,1) with finite n-skeleton for each n)?
justification: The draft is targeting exactly Question 3.5 in Section 3.3. The surrounding paragraph shows the intended scope very precisely: the motivation is the current gap between boundedly acyclic simple orderable groups already known in the literature and finitely presented simple orderable groups, which are known but not boundedly acyclic. The immediately preceding sentences also define the finiteness notation Fn and F∞, so the only real refinements needed are to make the quantifier explicit and to unpack the standard terminology if a completely stand-alone formulation is desired. There is no narrower or more official neighboring formulation than Question 3.5 itself.
